examples.problem:
Evaluate $\displaystyle \int_C \left(x^2 + y^2\right)\,\textrm d y,$ where $C$ is the path along the upper-right quarter of the circle $x^2 + y^2 = 4,$ traversed from the point $(2,0)$ to the point $(0,2),$ as shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14058598/assets/8fc3a36829c9780c34e13f253d607c3849bfd3ef1399a77a79a3dd3d30ef7140.png)
examples.worked_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
\int\limits_C f(x, y) \, \textrm{d}y = \int\limits_a^b  f(\mathbf r(t)) \, \dfrac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} \, \textrm{d}t.
$$

The curve $C$ is a quarter of a circle of radius $2$ centered at $O.$ It can be parameterized as 

$$
\mathbf{r}(t) = \big\langle 2\cos{t}, \: 2\sin{t} \big\rangle, \qquad 0 \le t \le \dfrac{\pi}{2}.
$$

Computing $\dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}t},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2\operatorname{sin}⁡t)=2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y) = x^2 + y^2$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =(2\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2}+(2\operatorname{sin}⁡t)^{2} \\  & =4({cos}^{2}⁡t+{sin}^{2}⁡t) \\  & =4.\end{aligned}
$$

We can now evaluate the integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}y & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}f(r(t))\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}4\cdot (2\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\cdot \text{d}t \\  & =8{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & =8\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,{|}_{0}^{\pi /2} \\  & =8\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})-8\operatorname{sin}⁡0 \\  & =8.\end{aligned}
$$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14058598/assets/8d55ece1948f9ecb7da7d489b86a297651a34f409f83ba2470f6dd06678a375e.png)

Which of the following is equivalent to ${\int }_{C}(x-y)\,\text{d}y,$ where $C$ is the path along a circle of radius $3,$ traversed from the point $(0,-3)$ to the point $(0,3),$ as shown above?

*Hint: Use the parametrization $r(t)=⟨3\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,3\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩.$*
feedback.worked_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}y={\int }_{a}^{b}f(r(t))\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t.
$$

 

The curve $C$ is a part-circle of radius $3$ centered at $O.$ It can be parameterized as 

$$
r(t)=⟨3\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,3\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩,\,-\frac{\pi }{2}\le t\le \frac{\pi }{2}.
$$

Computing $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3\operatorname{sin}⁡t)=3\operatorname{cos}⁡t\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)=x-y,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =3\operatorname{cos}⁡t-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t \\  & =3(\operatorname{cos}⁡t-\operatorname{sin}⁡t).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}y & ={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}f(r(t))\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}3(\operatorname{cos}⁡t-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\cdot 3\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & =9{\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$
